name: Audio-Visual Systems
title: Audio-Visual Systems
answer: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image are generated, processed or synchronised together, often in response to the presence or actions of an audience. The work spans gallery installations, live audiovisual performance, projection mapping, and responsive environments, and it sits between sound art, video art and creative coding. Practitioners typically come from media art, music technology and interaction design rather than from a single discipline, and the field overlaps with stage design, museum interpretation and public art commissioning.

sections.body: Audio-visual systems in interactive and experiential art are installations and performances where sound and moving image are generated, processed or synchronised together, often in response to the presence or actions of an audience. The work spans gallery installations, live audiovisual performance, projection mapping, and responsive environments, and it sits between sound art, video art and creative coding. Practitioners typically come from media art, music technology and interaction design rather than from a single discipline, and the field overlaps with stage design, museum interpretation and public art commissioning.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a computer or small cluster driving audio and video in the same session, with a shared clock so that sound and image stay aligned. Typical setups use a graphics pipeline for rendering, an audio engine for synthesis or playback, and a protocol such as OSC or MIDI to move control data between them. Sensors, cameras, microphones and depth trackers feed audience input into the system, and outputs go to projectors, LED walls, multichannel speaker arrays or headphones. Because the site tracks 2,000 audio models and 1,000 video models, many recent works draw on pretrained models for one or both streams rather than synthesising everything from scratch.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with a concept and a spatial plan, then moves into prototyping with creative coding environments such as Max, TouchDesigner, Pure Data or openFrameworks. Artists build a control layer that maps input to parameters, then tune the relationship between sound and image by hand, since perceptual synchrony is judged by eye and ear rather than by a specification. Rehearsal or gallery testing follows, because latency, projector alignment and room acoustics change how the piece reads. Documentation, cue lists and a stable build are prepared so the work can be shown again without the artist present at every moment.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions cluster around the source material: recorded music, film clips, photographs and voice, plus the training data behind any generative model used in the piece. Commissioning agreements, gallery contracts and performance licences usually set out who owns the resulting recordings and whether the work can be restaged or sold as an edition. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, which is a reminder that audio generation carries live legal exposure. Provenance practice includes keeping model versions, prompts, seeds and session files, and crediting collaborators, performers and any rights holders whose material is embedded in the work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter coupling between generated sound and generated image, with both streams conditioned on the same input so that they respond as one system rather than two. Real-time models are getting faster, which shifts more work from pre-rendered playback toward live generation in the room. At the same time, institutions are asking harder questions about energy use, hardware churn and the longevity of works that depend on specific model versions. Expect more attention to archiving the system itself, not just the recording, and to clearer terms for how generative audio-visual work is licensed and shown.
